clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of citrin, the liver-type mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate carrier encoded by SLC25A13, which supplies aspartate to the urea cycle and shuttles reducing equivalents via the malate-aspartate cycle.
Presents in an age-dependent spectrum: neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis (NICCD), a childhood phase with characteristic food preferences, and adult-onset citrullinaemia type 2 (CTLN2).
NICCD causes transient cholestatic jaundice, fatty liver, poor growth and multiple aminoacidaemias in infancy that often resolve spontaneously with supportive dietary measures.
Affected children characteristically prefer protein- and fat-rich foods and avoid carbohydrate-rich, sweet foods, an important diagnostic clue.

Adult CTLN2 presents with recurrent hyperammonaemic encephalopathy, disorientation, aberrant behaviour and neuropsychiatric symptoms, often precipitated by alcohol, certain medications or high carbohydrate intake.

Crucially, high-carbohydrate loading and glycerol- or fructose-containing infusions can worsen this disorder, in contrast to most other urea cycle defects, so a carbohydrate-restricted, higher-protein and higher-fat approach with medium-chain triglycerides is favoured.
Glycerol and fructose infusions and standard high-glucose regimens may precipitate deterioration and are generally contraindicated during crises.
Liver transplantation is effective for adult CTLN2 and prevents recurrent hyperammonaemic crises.
reference.pathophysiology: Citrin is the liver-specific mitochondrial aspartate-glutamate antiporter and an essential component of the malate-aspartate shuttle, which transfers cytosolic reducing equivalents into mitochondria and exports aspartate to the cytosol. Aspartate exported by citrin is the nitrogen donor that argininosuccinate synthetase combines with citrulline in the urea cycle; when citrin is deficient this cytosolic aspartate supply fails, so ureagenesis is impaired and citrulline and ammonia accumulate, producing a functional block distinct from the primary enzyme defect of classic citrullinaemia. Loss of the malate-aspartate shuttle also raises the cytosolic NADH to NAD+ ratio, impairing glycolysis and gluconeogenesis and making the liver intolerant of carbohydrate load, which explains why carbohydrate excess is deleterious and why patients instinctively favour protein and fat. In neonates the immature and stressed liver manifests cholestasis, steatosis and a generalised disturbance of amino acid metabolism (NICCD), which typically remits as metabolism matures. Years later, often after an apparently well period, a proportion of individuals develop adult-onset citrullinaemia type 2 with recurrent hyperammonaemia and neuropsychiatric decompensation, frequently unmasked by alcohol, drugs or dietary triggers. The tissue-specific expression of citrin accounts for the predominantly hepatic and metabolic, rather than purely urea-cycle, phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Citrullinaemia type 1 (ASS1 deficiency) and other primary urea cycle disorders
Neonatal cholestasis from biliary atresia, infection or other metabolic liver disease
Tyrosinaemia and galactosaemia in the infantile cholestatic presentation
Alcohol-related or drug-induced encephalopathy in adults
Primary psychiatric illness (for adult neuropsychiatric CTLN2)
Reye-like syndrome and fatty acid oxidation defects
Other causes of adult hyperammonaemic encephalopathy including hepatic failure
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids showing raised citrulline (and often threonine-to-serine ratio changes) and, in infancy, multiple aminoacidaemias
Plasma ammonia during symptomatic adult episodes
Liver function tests, coagulation and imaging for cholestasis and steatosis in infants
Serum and urine measurement of relevant metabolites and bile acids
Molecular genetic testing of the SLC25A13 gene
Assessment of dietary preference and carbohydrate tolerance
Fasting glucose and lactate to assess the redox and gluconeogenic disturbance
redFlags: Acute hyperammonaemic encephalopathy or altered behaviour in an adult with known or suspected citrin deficiency
Deterioration after high-carbohydrate intake or glycerol- or fructose-containing infusion
Neonatal cholestasis with failure to thrive and coagulopathy
Rapidly progressive neuropsychiatric change with hyperammonaemia
Signs of cerebral oedema during a hyperammonaemic crisis
reference.prognosis: NICCD usually resolves with supportive care and appropriate feeding, though a minority progress to significant liver disease. Adult-onset CTLN2 carries a risk of life-threatening hyperammonaemic crises, but avoidance of triggers, appropriate diet and, where needed, liver transplantation markedly improve outcome.
pitfalls: Managing crises with high-glucose or glycerol- or fructose-containing fluids as for other urea cycle disorders, which can worsen citrin deficiency
Recommending a low-protein, high-carbohydrate diet, which is counterproductive in this condition
Misdiagnosing adult CTLN2 as a primary psychiatric disorder or alcohol-related encephalopathy
Assuming NICCD that resolves in infancy means lifelong cure and missing later adult-onset disease
Confusing citrin deficiency with citrullinaemia type 1, which has different dietary and treatment implications
